prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the weakness to chemotherapy-related neuropathy, deconditioning or myasthenia gravis.
Do not prescribe amifampridine with a seizure history or with QT-prolonging drugs.

Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.
Do not conclude that there is no tumor on the basis of the chest CT alone.
required_recommendations: Diagnose paraneoplastic LEMS with a new small cell lung cancer and refer urgently to oncology for staging (including brain MRI) and treatment, which often improves the LEMS.

Start amifampridine 15 mg/day in divided doses, titrating to effect up to 60 mg/day (EU maximum), with an ECG before the first dose and at least yearly during treatment (EU SmPC), and counseling on seizure risk and paresthesias.
Add pyridostigmine if the response to amifampridine is incomplete, watching heart rate because he takes metoprolol; reserve IVIG for severe or rapidly progressive weakness.
Review every new drug for QT prolongation (for example chemotherapy antiemetics) before combining it with amifampridine.
Inform the anesthesiologist before any further procedure under general anesthesia (for example port insertion or mediastinoscopy) that he has LEMS, because of sensitivity to neuromuscular blockers.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in a neuromuscular junction disorder.
CSF has no diagnostic role in LEMS; there is no sign of central or meningeal involvement.

accepted: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), paraneoplastic, secondary to new small cell lung cancer (SCLC); anti-VGCC P/Q-type positive, anti-SOX1 positive
LEMS with small cell lung cancer

differential.key_features: MG gives normal baseline CMAPs without post-exercise facilitation; here CMAPs are low with a 142-152% increment, VGCC antibodies are positive and AChR and MuSK are negative.
Normal CK, reduced reflexes and post-exercise facilitation do not fit a myopathy.
Explains the reduced sural SNAPs and foot numbness, which coexist, but not proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms or facilitation.
Botulism is acute and descending with early ocular and bulbar signs; this is a 4-month proximal syndrome without exposure.
He takes atorvastatin, but CK is normal and a myopathy does not cause low CMAPs with post-exercise facilitation.

P/Q-type VGCC and SOX1 antibodies with small cell lung cancer can also cause cerebellar degeneration, and he has a wide-based gait and mildly impaired heel-shin; finger-nose is normal, eye movements are full and the speech change is fatigable rather than ataxic, so hip flexor weakness and the distal sensory neuropathy explain the gait. Reassess if limb ataxia or nystagmus appears.

key_clinical_evidence: Proximal leg weakness with reduced reflexes that improve after brief exercise, dry mouth and erectile dysfunction: the LEMS triad.
Low baseline CMAPs with 142-152% increment after 10 s of maximal contraction: a presynaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission.
P/Q-type VGCC antibodies positive; SOX1 antibodies positive, favoring small cell lung cancer. DELTA-P score 3 (speech, erectile dysfunction, age 50 or older): high probability of SCLC.
A 50 pack-year smoker with a previous lung cancer: a negative chest CT does not end the tumor search; FDG-PET shows an avid hilar node and biopsy shows small cell carcinoma, a new primary.
Amifampridine is the symptomatic treatment; tumor treatment often improves the syndrome.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Negative AChR antibodies do not exclude a presynaptic disorder; P/Q-type VGCC antibodies identify LEMS.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude that a neuromuscular junction disorder is excluded.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: CT misses small or normal-sized nodal disease; with SOX1 antibodies FDG-PET is indicated, and screening continues for 2 years if negative.
red_herrings.data_point: CT chest with no mass and a hilar node not enlarged by size criteria
red_herrings.intended_effect: Stop the tumor search after a negative CT.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A length-dependent sensory neuropathy explains the foot numbness but not proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms or post-exercise facilitation.
red_herrings.data_point: Previous cisplatin-based chemotherapy and distal sensory loss with reduced sural SNAPs
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the weakness to chemotherapy-related neuropathy.

contraindications: Amifampridine: epilepsy or history of seizures; congenital long QT syndrome; concomitant drugs with a known potential to prolong the QT interval (EU SmPC); concomitant drugs with a narrow therapeutic window.

interactions: Amifampridine + apixaban: no known pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction.
Amifampridine + metoprolol, lisinopril, metformin, atorvastatin, cyanocobalamin: no clinically relevant interaction; none of these drugs has known QT-prolonging potential.
amifampridine.summary: No interaction with current medicines; observe the QT and seizure restrictions.
warnings: Dose-related seizure risk; start 15 mg/day in divided doses, increase by 5 mg every 4-5 days, EU maximum 60 mg/day.
Clinical and ECG monitoring at initiation and yearly thereafter (EU SmPC); ECG at once if symptoms suggest arrhythmia.
Perioral and acral paresthesias are common and dose related.
Check later additions against the QT restriction (for example 5-HT3 antiemetics during chemotherapy).

results.finding: LEMS presents with proximal leg weakness, autonomic symptoms and reduced reflexes; P/Q-type VGCC antibodies are found in most patients; about half have an associated small cell lung cancer; amifampridine is the symptomatic treatment of choice and tumor treatment improves the syndrome.
results.source: Titulaer MJ, Lang B, Verschuuren JJ, Lancet Neurol 2011;10:1098-1107 (review)

results.finding: CT of the thorax is the first screening test, followed by FDG-PET if negative; screening is repeated every 3-6 months for 2 years.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al., Eur J Neurol 2011;18:19-e3 (EFNS guideline on paraneoplastic screening)

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome diagno.summary: Titulaer MJ et al. (Lancet Neurol 2011;10:1098-1107) describe LEMS as proximal weakness, autonomic dysfunction and areflexia with P/Q-type VGCC antibodies in about 85-90%; about half of patients have small cell lung cancer. SOX1 antibodies favour an associated SCLC. CT of the thorax is the first screening study and FDG-PET is added when CT is negative, with repeat screening every 3-6 months for 2 years (EFNS 2011). Amifampridine is the first-line symptomatic treatment.

patient.history_present_illness: A 72-year-old former smoker with treated non-small cell lung cancer in remission (squamous cell, stage II, right upper lobectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy 3 years ago) presented for evaluation of progressive proximal leg weakness over 4 months. He initially noticed difficulty rising from low chairs and climbing stairs approximately 4 months ago. He attributed this to deconditioning after his cancer treatment. Over 2 months, the weakness progressed to difficulty rising from the toilet without the safety rail and climbing stairs required use of the handrail. He denies ptosis or diplopia. His wife reports his voice becomes slightly slurred after dinner conversations lasting more than 20 minutes. He has also had increasing dryness of the mouth over the past 6 months, which he attributed to his medication side effects. He mentioned to his urologist that he had developed erectile dysfunction approximately 6 months ago. He does not have significant sensory symptoms in his hands but notices mild numbness and tingling in his feet. His deep tendon reflexes were noted to be diminished at a recent appointment. His last surveillance CT chest, 6 months ago, showed no evidence of recurrence. He was initially referred to physical therapy for 'deconditioning' without improvement. Oncology attributed his weakness to chemotherapy-related peripheral neuropathy and added B12 supplementation. He was referred to neurology because the weakness kept progressing.

neurological_exam.additional: No ptosis or diplopia. Proximal more than distal leg weakness. Dry mouth with reduced saliva pooling. No respiratory distress.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: No ptosis at rest. No diplopia. Eye movements full. Pupils 3 mm, equal and reactive. Mild facial weakness. No dysarthria at rest; speech becomes mildly slurred after 5 minutes of sustained speech. Gag reflex present.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Cooperative. Appropriate affect.
neurological_exam.motor: Hip flexors 3+/5 bilaterally, shoulder abductors 4-/5 bilaterally, distal strength 5/5. Hip flexion strength improves transiently after a few seconds of repeated maximal effort. No fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps, triceps, patellar and Achilles reflexes 1+ and symmetric; the patellar reflex becomes brisker after 10 seconds of maximal quadriceps contraction. Plantar responses flexor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mild stocking-glove decrease to light touch and vibration in feet and ankles bilaterally. Proprioception intact in toes.

physical_exam.general: Weight 83.5 kg, height 178 cm. Irregularly irregular pulse, rate controlled. Lungs clear.
